presentingComplaint: Progressive abdominal distension, leg swelling and jaundice over 3 weeks
history: 54-year-old man with a 15-year history of heavy alcohol intake (approx 80 g/day) presents with gradually worsening abdominal swelling, bilateral ankle oedema and yellowing of the eyes over 3 weeks. Reduced appetite, early satiety and 4 kg apparent weight gain despite poor intake. No haematemesis or melaena. Mild intermittent confusion in the evenings noted by family. Known esophageal varices on prior endoscopy; not on beta-blocker. No recent GI bleed, sepsis or new medications. No fever.
examination: Icteric sclerae, palmar erythema, multiple spider naevi over the chest, gynaecomastia. Abdomen distended with shifting dullness and a fluid thrill consistent with moderate-to-tense ascites; non-tender, no guarding (pertinent negative - no peritonism to suggest SBP). Splenomegaly palpable. Mild asterixis elicited. Bilateral pitting pedal oedema. No focal neurological deficit. Chest clear, no basal crackles (pertinent negative against cardiac failure).

labs.Ascitic fluid: SAAG 1.6 g/dL, protein 0.8 g/dL, PMN 90 cells/mm3 (<250, no SBP)

imaging: Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler: coarse, nodular, shrunken liver with surface irregularity, splenomegaly (15 cm), recanalised paraumbilical vein and patent but dilated portal vein consistent with portal hypertension; moderate ascites. No focal liver mass; portal vein patent (no thrombosis).
microbiology: Ascitic fluid culture negative; blood cultures not indicated (afebrile, PMN <250)
differentialDiagnoses: Decompensated cirrhosis with ascites and early hepatic encephalopathy
finalDiagnosis: Decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis (ascites + hepatic encephalopathy, Child-Pugh C)
citations: AASLD Management of Ascites due to Cirrhosis 2021
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective decompensation. Ascitic PMN <250/mm3 and afebrile, so no empiric antibiotics indicated. Reserve antibiotic prophylaxis/treatment for confirmed SBP (PMN >=250) or GI bleed.
contraindications: Avoid NSAIDs (precipitate AKI/hepatorenal syndrome and GI bleed)
Avoid nephrotoxins and aminoglycosides given borderline renal function
Dose-adjust renally cleared drugs; avoid hepatotoxins
edgeCases: Ascitic PMN >=250/mm3 would reclassify as SBP requiring cefotaxime and albumin
Rapidly rising creatinine after diuresis/paracentesis may signal hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI)
A new focal liver lesion on imaging mandates HCC surveillance (AFP + triphasic CT/MRI)
expectedMaiK: This is a classic decompensated cirrhosis picture - ascites (SAAG >=1.1), coagulopathy, hypoalbuminaemia, thrombocytopenia and early encephalopathy on an alcohol-related background. It is non-infective: with ascitic PMN <250 and no fever there is no indication for empiric antibiotics; prioritise diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP, sodium/fluid restriction with spironolactone-based diuresis, and lactulose for encephalopathy.
expectedNextQuestions: Any recent GI bleeding (haematemesis, melaena) or missed lactulose doses?
Alcohol quantity and time since last drink; any withdrawal symptoms?
Fever, abdominal pain or constipation that could point to SBP or a precipitant?
expectedInvestigations: Diagnostic ascitic tap with cell count, SAAG and culture
Serum electrolytes, creatinine and MELD-Na for prognosis
Upper GI endoscopy for variceal surveillance

investigations: Diagnostic ascitic tap (cell count, SAAG, culture)

regressionAssertions: stewardship tier must be null (non-infective - no empiric antibiotics)
SBP must appear in differential given ascites but not be the top diagnosis (PMN <250)
